[Beyond the Scrum Guide] = from the Agile Manifesto, or from Scrum Alliance's description of the values, or the mapping between them and Scrum. The Guide itself does not mention the Manifesto.

toc.title: Exam Traps and What the Exam Expects

html:
1The Five Scrum Values (SF 1.2)

The Guide: "Successful use of Scrum depends on people becoming more proficient in living five values: Commitment, Focus, Openness, Respect, and Courage."

Value What the Guide says Scrum Alliance's description Beyond the Guide
Commitment The Scrum Team commits to achieving its goals and to supporting each other Teams trust each other to follow through on what they say they will do
Focus Their primary focus is on the work of the Sprint to make the best possible progress toward the goals Everyone concentrates on the work at hand to support the Sprint Goal
Openness The Scrum Team and its stakeholders are open about the work and the challenges Teams look for new ideas and opportunities to learn and are open about needing help
Respect Members respect each other to be capable, independent people, and are respected as such by the people they work with People respect one another, the Product Owner, the Scrum Master and stakeholders, and value each contribution
Courage The members have the courage to do the right thing and to work on tough problems Teams feel safe enough to say no, ask for help, try new things and challenge norms that block success

Memory aid: commit, focus, be open, respect, have courage. Questions often add false values such as transparency, trust, collaboration, discipline or accountability.

1.1 What the Guide says the values do

  • The values "give direction to the Scrum Team with regard to their work, actions, and behavior."
  • "The decisions that are made, the steps taken, and the way Scrum is used should reinforce these values, not diminish or undermine them."
  • Team members "learn and explore the values as they work with the Scrum events and artifacts."
  • When the values are embodied by the Scrum Team and the people they work with, the empirical pillars of transparency, inspection and adaptation come to life, building trust.
Exam angle

in a scenario, the best answer usually strengthens a value (openness about a problem, courage to say no to lower quality, focus on the Sprint Goal). A choice that hides bad news, accepts every request or splits the team's attention undermines the values and is wrong.

1.2 Where each value shows up Beyond the Guide

Value Typical places in Scrum
Commitment The Sprint Goal (a commitment by the Developers), the Definition of Done, supporting each other to reach the goal
Focus The Sprint Goal creates "coherence and focus"; the Daily Scrum focuses on progress toward the Sprint Goal; working in Sprints at a sustainable pace "improves the Scrum Team's focus and consistency"
Openness Transparent artifacts; honest talk at the Daily Scrum, the Sprint Review and the Retrospective; sharing impediments early
Respect Collaborative Sprint Planning; the whole organization respecting the Product Owner's decisions; no blaming in the Retrospective
Courage Telling a stakeholder that an item will not fit; refusing to count unfinished work as Done; raising hard problems in the Retrospective

2Values and the Pillars

Pillars Values
What they are The three parts of empiricism: transparency, inspection, adaptation Five qualities of behavior: commitment, focus, openness, respect, courage
Role Make the process empirical Give the team direction and make the pillars work by building trust
Example The artifacts are visible and inspected at each event The team is open about a problem it found when inspecting

Values are what make the pillars real: without openness there is no transparency, and without courage a team does not adapt when inspection shows an uncomfortable truth.

3The Agile Manifesto (SF 1.7)

The Manifesto for Agile Software Development was written in February 2001 by seventeen practitioners, among them Scrum's creators Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland. It has four values and twelve principles. The Scrum Guide does not mention it, but the learning objectives and Scrum Alliance's own description of Scrum rest on it: Scrum is considered agile because it reflects the Manifesto.

3.1 The four values

The authors state that they value the items on the left more than those on the right. The items on the right still have value.

The Manifesto values What it means How Scrum reflects it Beyond the Guide
Individuals and interactions over processes and tools People and how they work together matter more than the tools and procedures The rules of Scrum "guide their relationships and interactions" instead of giving detailed instructions; the team is self-managing
Working software over comprehensive documentation A usable product is the best evidence of progress Every Sprint produces a usable Increment that meets the Definition of Done
Customer collaboration over contract negotiation Work with the customer throughout, instead of fixing everything in a contract at the start Stakeholders collaborate at the Sprint Review; the Product Owner keeps the Product Backlog current
Responding to change over following a plan Adapt when you learn something new The Product Backlog is emergent; every event is a chance to inspect and adapt; the Sprint Backlog is updated daily

3.2 The twelve principles

The principles are paraphrased here; the exact wording is on agilemanifesto.org.

# Principle (paraphrased) Where Scrum shows it Beyond the Guide
1 Satisfy the customer through early and continuous delivery of valuable software An Increment every Sprint; the Product Owner maximizes the value of the product
2 Welcome changing requirements, even late, for the customer's advantage The Product Backlog is emergent and can be reordered at any time; the Review may adjust it "to meet new opportunities"
3 Deliver working software frequently, preferring the shorter timescale Sprints of one month or less; shorter Sprints "generate more learning cycles"
4 Business people and developers work together daily The Scrum Team is responsible for stakeholder collaboration; the Product Owner and Developers refine and plan together
5 Build projects around motivated individuals, give them support and trust them The Scrum Team is "structured and empowered by the organization to manage their own work"; members are respected "to be capable, independent people"
6 Face-to-face conversation is the most efficient way to share information Events bring the whole team together; the Daily Scrum is held at the same time and place; the Review is a working session
7 Working software is the primary measure of progress An Increment must be usable; work that does not meet the Definition of Done is not part of it
8 Promote sustainable development: a constant pace indefinitely "Working in Sprints at a sustainable pace improves the Scrum Team's focus and consistency"
9 Continuous attention to technical excellence and good design The Developers are accountable for "instilling quality by adhering to a Definition of Done"; quality does not decrease during the Sprint
10 Simplicity: maximizing the amount of work not done Lean thinking "focuses on the essentials"; an ordered Product Backlog; "Scrum is simple"
11 The best designs emerge from self-organizing teams Developers decide how to turn items into Increments, "at the sole discretion of the Developers"
12 At regular intervals the team reflects and adjusts its behavior The Sprint Retrospective at the end of every Sprint
Exam angle

a question about alignment is answered by matching a Manifesto idea with the Scrum feature that carries it: working software → Increment and Definition of Done; responding to change → emergent Product Backlog; reflection → Retrospective; self-organizing teams → self-managing Scrum Team; frequent delivery → short Sprints.

3.3 Scrum and the Manifesto compared

Agile Manifesto Scrum
What it is Four values and twelve principles: a mindset A framework with accountabilities, events, artifacts and rules
Prescribes events or roles? No Yes: five events, three accountabilities, three artifacts
Source for the exam Learning objectives (SF 1.7) The Scrum Guide and the learning objectives
Answers the question Why work this way? How to do it, inside a few rules

4Exam Traps and What the Exam Expects

  1. Values versus pillars. Values: commitment, focus, openness, respect, courage. Pillars: transparency, inspection, adaptation. Adding "trust" or "transparency" to the values is a trap.
  2. Respect is about capable, independent people. It is not about politeness alone; it supports self-management.
  3. The Manifesto "values the left more", not "only the left". Processes, tools, documentation, contracts and plans are not rejected.
  4. The Manifesto is not Scrum. It has no events or roles. Scrum implements its ideas.
  5. Four values, twelve principles. Keep the counts apart from Scrum's five values and three pillars.
  6. Alignment answers connect a Manifesto statement to a specific Scrum feature. "Scrum follows the Manifesto because it is agile" is circular and weak.
  7. Values guide decisions. In scenarios, reject answers that hide problems (openness), avoid hard truths (courage), scatter attention (focus), blame people (respect) or drop the team's goals (commitment).
  8. Sustainable pace is a principle and also in the Guide: Sprints at a sustainable pace improve focus and consistency. "Work overtime to finish the Sprint" contradicts it.

5Exam Q&A

5.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1A Developer discovers on day three of the Sprint that a planned item is much harder than expected, but the team is proud of its record and nobody wants to say so. Which Scrum value should the Scrum Master help the team practise most?

  • AOpenness, by sharing the problem and the challenge with the team and the Product Owner
  • BRespect, by making sure nobody criticizes the Developer
  • CCommitment, by insisting that the original plan is kept
  • DFocus, by asking the team to work harder on the item
Show the answer

Answer: A. The Scrum Team and its stakeholders are open about the work and the challenges. Sharing the problem early lets the Developers adapt the plan and negotiate scope with the Product Owner without endangering the Sprint Goal. Keeping the plan at any cost or working harder hides the problem.

S2A stakeholder asks the Product Owner to add an extra feature to the Sprint, and the Product Owner is about to say yes to avoid conflict. Which value would help the Product Owner most?

  • ACourage, to say no or to discuss the request openly
  • BCommitment, to accept every request
  • CRespect, to give stakeholders what they ask for
  • DFocus, to ignore the stakeholder
Show the answer

Answer: A. The values include the courage to do the right thing and to work on tough problems, which includes saying no or negotiating. Accepting every request undermines the Sprint Goal and the Developers' commitment. Ignoring the stakeholder is not respect.

S3Which list contains only Scrum values?

  • ATransparency, inspection, adaptation, courage, respect
  • BCommitment, focus, openness, respect, courage
  • CTrust, collaboration, courage, focus, commitment
  • DCommitment, discipline, transparency, respect, openness
Show the answer

Answer: B. The Guide names exactly five values: commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage. Transparency, inspection and adaptation are the pillars, and trust, collaboration and discipline are not Scrum values.

S4A Scrum Team wants to explain to its organization how Scrum reflects the Manifesto statement "responding to change over following a plan". Which feature fits best?

  • AThe Daily Scrum is held at the same time and place every working day, which gives the team a steady and predictable rhythm
  • BThe Scrum Team has three accountabilities, which makes it clear who is responsible for each decision in the framework
  • CThe Product Backlog is emergent and can be reordered, and each event is an opportunity to inspect and adapt
  • DSprints are of fixed length, so the team always knows exactly how much time it has to finish a planned set of work
Show the answer

Answer: C. An emergent Product Backlog and events built for inspection and adaptation are how Scrum responds to change. A fixed Sprint length and a fixed schedule for the Daily Scrum create regularity but do not answer the statement, and accountabilities do not speak to change.

S5A manager says that because the Manifesto prefers "working software over comprehensive documentation", the team should stop documenting anything. What is the best reply?

  • AAgree, because documentation has no value in Scrum and the Definition of Done should never include it
  • BAgree, but only for the first few Sprints, until the team has built enough working software to need documents
  • CExplain that the Manifesto still values the items on the right, and the team decides which documentation its Definition of Done needs
  • DDisagree, because Scrum requires a detailed document for every Increment before it can be shown to stakeholders at the Sprint Review and released
Show the answer

Answer: C. The Manifesto values the left items more but does not say the right items have no value. Scrum does not prescribe documentation either way. The Developers adhere to a Definition of Done that reflects the quality measures required for the product, which may include documentation.

S6A new team works overtime every Sprint to finish everything it planned. Which Manifesto principle and Guide statement does this go against?

  • AFrequent delivery, because overtime makes Sprints longer
  • BCustomer collaboration, because customers dislike overtime
  • CSimplicity, because overtime adds work
  • DA sustainable pace, because working in Sprints at a sustainable pace improves focus and consistency
Show the answer

Answer: D. The Manifesto promotes sustainable development at a constant pace, and the Guide says that working in Sprints at a sustainable pace improves the Scrum Team's focus and consistency. Overtime to hit a plan is not a sustainable pace.

S7In a Retrospective a Developer wants to raise a conflict with a colleague, but fears the reaction. Which two values should the Scrum Master help the team strengthen?

  • ACommitment and focus
  • BOpenness and courage
  • CRespect and focus
  • DCourage and commitment
Show the answer

Answer: B. Raising a hard problem needs the courage to do the right thing and openness about the work and its challenges. Respect also matters, but the pair that fits the situation best is openness and courage.

S8A trainer says that the Manifesto's twelve principles are the twelve Scrum rules. What is the best correction?

  • AThe twelve principles are the twelve rules of the Scrum Guide, which is why every Scrum Team has to follow all of them in every Sprint it runs
  • BThe principles belong to Scrum Alliance, not to Scrum, so they appear in its learning objectives but nowhere else
  • CThe principles are written for the Scrum Master only, who passes them on to the team as working rules
  • DThe Manifesto is a mindset of four values and twelve principles; Scrum is a framework that reflects them with its own events
Show the answer

Answer: D. The Manifesto has no roles or events. Scrum has its own definition in the Scrum Guide and reflects the Manifesto's ideas through its framework.

5.2 Recall Q&As

R1What are the five Scrum values?

Show the answer

Commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage.

R2What does the Guide say the values do for the Scrum Team?

Show the answer

They give direction regarding work, actions and behavior, and the way Scrum is used should reinforce them. When embodied, they bring the empirical pillars to life and build trust.

R3How does the Guide describe the value of Respect?

Show the answer

Scrum Team members respect each other to be capable, independent people, and are respected as such by the people they work with.

R4How does the Guide describe Courage?

Show the answer

The Scrum Team members have the courage to do the right thing and to work on tough problems.

R5How does the Guide describe Openness?

Show the answer

The Scrum Team and its stakeholders are open about the work and the challenges.

R6How does the Guide describe Focus?

Show the answer

The primary focus is the work of the Sprint, to make the best possible progress toward the team's goals.

R7How does the Guide describe Commitment?

Show the answer

The Scrum Team commits to achieving its goals and to supporting each other.

R8Which are pillars and which are values?

Show the answer

Pillars: transparency, inspection, adaptation. Values: commitment, focus, openness, respect, courage.

R9What are the four values of the Agile Manifesto?

Show the answer

Individuals and interactions over processes and tools; working software over comprehensive documentation; customer collaboration over contract negotiation; responding to change over following a plan.

R10What does the Manifesto say about the items on the right?

Show the answer

They have value, but the items on the left are valued more.

R11How many principles does the Manifesto have?

Show the answer

Twelve.

R12Name three ways Scrum reflects the Manifesto.

Show the answer

A usable Increment every Sprint (working software); an emergent Product Backlog and events built to inspect and adapt (responding to change); a self-managing Scrum Team (self-organizing teams); the Retrospective (regular reflection); short Sprints (frequent delivery).

R13Does the Scrum Guide mention the Agile Manifesto?

Show the answer

No. The Manifesto is named by the learning objectives as a source of the exam.

6Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Values (5) Commitment · Focus · Openness · Respect · Courage
Commitment Commits to its goals and supports each other
Focus Primary focus on the work of the Sprint
Openness Open about the work and the challenges
Respect Each other as capable, independent people
Courage Do the right thing; work on tough problems
Values do Give direction; the way Scrum is used should reinforce them; make the pillars work and build trust
Values vs pillars Values: five behaviors. Pillars: transparency, inspection, adaptation
Manifesto (Feb 2001) 4 values + 12 principles; left valued more, right still has value
Manifesto values Individuals and interactions · working software · customer collaboration · responding to change
Alignment Working software → Increment and Definition of Done · change → emergent Product Backlog · reflection → Retrospective · self-organization → self-managing team · frequent delivery → short Sprints
Not the same The Manifesto is a mindset; Scrum is a framework with roles, events and artifacts
